title: Robots.txt Is Not Access Control: RFC 9309 Explained
seoTitle: Robots.txt, Noindex and Access Control: RFC 9309
subtitle: Choose the control that matches the outcome you need.
seoDescription: Separate robots.txt from noindex, authentication, authorization and rate limits. Test deployed policy without treating bot headers as verified identity.

artwork.alt: A ceremonial paper boundary gives way to progressively stronger barriers protecting a monochrome vault.
artwork.label: Crawler policy / access boundary
artwork.caption: A published courtesy rule and a materially secured resource are different control layers.

author: SULAYMAN BOWLES
thesis: Robots.txt guides cooperating crawlers. Server-side authorization protects private content, and capacity controls limit costly work; neither should trust a claimed user agent as identity.

conclusion.title: Test each boundary separately
conclusion.content: Fetch the deployed robots policy, then test private access and capacity limits independently. Observed logs can establish which requests and responses reached that layer—not universal compliance, verified provider identity from a token, or downstream use.

evidenceBoundary: The controls in this article describe publisher-side policy and enforcement. A rule does not prove that every client complies, that a provider attributed a request the same way, or that an allowed page will be crawled, indexed, trained on, or cited.
content: Deleting robots.txt should not expose a private document. RFC 9309 explicitly says its rules are not access authorization: the public file asks cooperating crawlers how to request paths on a service. A client that ignores it can still send ordinary HTTP requests. The file supplies no credential, firewall, encryption, or verified identity.

Crawl guidance, index processing, private access, and capacity protection need different controls. Robots directives express preferences to supporting systems; authentication identifies a principal; authorization checks permission; edge and application controls limit work. Logs then provide evidence about requests, not a substitute for enforcement.

sections.title: What the primary sources establish
paragraphs: This is a protocol interpretation, not provider documentation. The source ledger points to RFC 9309 section 3 and Google Search Central, reread for this source map on September 10, 2026. Other source dates retain their original cutoffs.

table.caption: Primary documentation for crawler policy and access control
rows: Publishing robots rules does not secure a resource; use an application-layer security control.
That every client follows the rules or that paths in robots.txt are private.
Robots rules manage cooperative crawling; a blocked URL may still appear in search.
A guarantee of deindexing or confidentiality.

sections.title: Match the outcome to the layer
paragraphs: First decide whether you need crawler guidance, index-processing preferences, private access, or capacity protection. Use robots.txt, noindex, authentication with authorization, or rate and concurrency limits accordingly; they do not enforce the same boundary.

Discovery policy communicates path rules through robots.txt. Document-processing policy uses meta elements or response headers to ask supporting indexers not to index fetched content or expose certain features. Authentication establishes a principal; authorization checks whether that principal may perform the action.

Capacity controls include connection and rate limits, quotas, caching, circuit breakers, and workload isolation. Observation uses logs, challenges, published address ranges, and response evidence to classify requests. Classification can inform enforcement, but a dashboard label cannot protect a route.

Write requirements in operational terms: avoid crawler work on facets, keep account documents private, permit search discovery while declining a named model-development crawler, or keep the origin healthy under bursts. Each requires its own combination of layers.

sections.title: Version the robots parser and its observations
paragraphs: RFC 9309 specifies user-agent and rule matching, access results, and caching. Test casing, group selection, percent-encoding, longest matches, comments, empty rules, Unicode, and retrieval failures with fixtures. Substring matching cannot implement that contract.

Scope policy to the serving service, preserving scheme, host, and port distinctions. Record redirects and caches: stale or cross-host files can differ from inspected source control. Save bytes, effective URL, status, retrieval time, parser version, selected group, and matching rule.

Missing, unreachable, or invalid policy differs from an explicit Allow or Disallow. Keep protocol-derived results separate from conservative local overrides, so changing operator policy does not rewrite the remote observation.
bullets: Fetch the production file from every relevant scheme, host, and port combination.
Keep the raw policy artifact and its redirect chain.
Version parser fixtures against the standard and known edge cases.
Record the selected group and exact matching rule for each decision.
Expire cached policy deliberately and expose stale-policy state.

sections.title: Make privacy independent of robots rules
paragraphs: Remove the robots file and change the client’s User-Agent: does the server still deny protected content? If not, that boundary does not make it private. Validate a principal and check resource permission on every request, denying by default when no rule grants access.

Disallowed paths are not secrets. The public file can reveal them, and links, logs, referrers, sitemaps, or prior crawls can expose them independently. Unauthorized requests must not receive the protected representation.

Use HTTP responses appropriate to the application and standard, then test actual access. Status alone is insufficient: alternate methods, encodings, hosts, cache keys, file variants, and indirect endpoints must not yield the representation to an unauthenticated or unauthorized requester.

table.caption: Outcome-to-control mapping
rows: Robots policy or URL inventory repair
Production policy and request logs reviewed
Remove a public page from an index
Published ranges and reverse checks when available

sections.title: Separate claimed and attributed identity
paragraphs: Anyone can send a familiar crawler token. User-Agent remains useful for log routing and robots-group selection, but cannot safely grant privileges or bypass expensive-request limits. Authenticate more strongly or keep the policy safe when identity is unknown.

Provider address ranges and verification guidance are dated attribution evidence. Retrieve them securely, validate the format, record version or hash, compare observed addresses, and specify stale or unavailable-feed behavior. Network ownership may support classification without proving a request’s purpose.

Log observed address, TLS and request properties, time, host, path, and full User-Agent separately from the claimed token. Keep attributed identity as a derived conclusion with method and confidence. A string match should not become a verified traffic count.

codeExamples.title: Verify policy and authorization as independent checks
codeExamples.description: The public policy response and protected-resource denial should both be tested.
codeExamples.code:
curl -fsS -D robots.headers https://example.com/robots.txt -o robots.body

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  -A "ExampleCrawler/1.0" https://example.com/private/account

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  -A "Mozilla/5.0" https://example.com/private/account

sections.title: Verify the deployed file and the protected routes
paragraphs: Before changing policy, review all user-agent groups, path rules, search rules, sitemaps, and inherited edge controls. Changes can affect discovery, indexing workflows, origin load, data use, and user-triggered retrieval. Structured generation can keep hosts and environments aligned.

Fetch production rather than inspecting a local copy. Check status, content type, group selection, sitemap host, redirects, and caching. Parse representative allowed and disallowed paths, then test authorization and capacity boundaries independently. Passing robots checks cannot establish private-route protection.

Logs show tokens, statuses, and rate-control events at the measured layer. They omit requests that never reached it, cannot verify full provider identity from a token, and do not reveal indexing or training decisions. Keep these gaps explicit instead of treating silence as compliance.
bullets: Review every existing group before merging a new crawler policy.
Test the deployed file from outside the origin environment.
Run parser fixtures against representative site paths.
Test private resources with no credentials and wrong credentials.
Measure origin rejections and latency after capacity-policy changes.
Date every provider-specific identity source and attribution rule.
